It's between Pokemon Red/Blue and Harvest Moon 64.

I have such vivid memories of the late 90's Pokemon craze that it's difficult to imagine anything else taking that crown. As a kid, the concept of collecting and training a battalion of monsters then competing and trading with friends was all-consuming. It was wonderful having an interest that was all but certain to be common among kids your age, male or female. However...

The Harvest Moon series, especially the title for N64, will always be special to me. Nobody ever thought that a farming simulator could be fun and addicting as hell at the time (then Farmville came 15 years later and shat on the genre. But I'm not bitter!). There were so many intricacies to the game and secrets to find while it maintained the relatively simple goal of managing the farm. The graphics were pretty outdated, even for the time it came out. But they, along with the characters, the poorly translated text, and the music made it an irresistably charming game. I have put more hours into it than any other single game, and it will probably always be my favorite and what I remember when I think of gaming as a child. I still play at least once a year.

For me, it was Nerf Arena Blast. There were other games that I played religiously (the Pokémon and Diablo franchises come to mind), but NAB really sticks out as one of my favorites.

If you've never heard of it, it's basically Unreal Tournament [99] with Nerf weapons (the CTF map Hall of Giants was remixed, amongst others, for use in NAB). It was even made using Unreal Engine 1 and the map-making community used Unreal Editor to create their maps.

This game was responsible for an initial love of computer creation, rather than just utilization for things like games or basic web-design. I was manipulating maps, learning how to shape objects, and do some basic programming. To that point, I had done some C++ and VB, but nothing that really sparked my interest.

How does a game do that?

The community was (and is) really friendly; people who made maps encouraged teamwork and partnerships. Everyone was always trying to take the game to the next level (user SLAM created a map out of the level lobby that basically teleported users to "different maps," an unhard of in this game).

Besides, it was ultra violent. The game used Nerf weapons, alongside some additional energy weapons. As such, nobody was killed, but simply disintegrated in a kind of holographic state and respawned a few seconds later.

I don't recall the game ever having the same mass following as UT, but I count that as a good thing. Everyone knew everyone, and for a kid that didn't really get on well with children IRL, my gaming buddies were a godsend. I learned how to make doors and elevators move within my maps, apply textures correctly, and even worked with some of NAB's first user AI-mapping attempts.

Finally, this period was the peak of my gaming abilities. I was able to destroy in my heyday. This extended into UT: GOTY when I finally got it, and I felt some sort of accomplishment actually being good at something and being recognized by my peers. My "high point" was when the NAB community added one of my noob-ish maps, (Stadium '01, to server rotations). I no longer have the same reflexes and fighting abilities I had back then, so I look back on my mo-mo-mo-mo-monster kill, kill, kills using my Triple Strike in PointBlast arenas.

Ugh, such a good game. Maybe a bit underrated.

If you're interested in playing it, a small community still exists, which even got the NAB rights from ATARI. You can now get NAB and a community mod-pack that significantly enhances the game.

tl;dr: Nerf Arena Blast meant more to me than just a fun game to play.

By asking questions to discover what is known, what is known by you, and what is unknown in both cases. Reading about classical and modern philosophers, all of whose works are public domain, help you frame different ways of thinking. My personal favorite is Socrates, but careful trying to emulate him. I've been banned from places that way. Oh, sweet irony...

Your first example is a philosophical "the map is not the territory". You have a map of ideas, in your mind, which appear consistent with all the other information you have. Yet, having not done it, you've only looked at the map and not the place itself. This is inconsequential in most cases because consistency is the very means by which we test reality, or sanity.

What is reality then? Think about dreams. Our lives are consistent while awake, but how do we know what is consistent from what is not? Dreams. Our dreams are what make reality seem real, for without them we'd have no comparison for something inconsistent.

The philosophy of empiricism relies exclusively on the fact reality, so far as has been observed, is consistent. It has rules which function, sometimes within ranges of probability, but nevertheless are consistent about it. An electron does not suddenly become "achaotic" then back to "chaotic" in its orbitals, much like fire does not become water.

How a philosopher would weigh truth, then, is by determining whether what has been learned is consistent. Socrates continuously accomplishes this by simply asking questions and, later, revealing the hypocrisy of many ideas. It is why he only knows that he knows nothing: Nothing he ever questions proves itself to be consistent. This is explicitly because all of his discussions deal with ideas, philosophy, and not observable realities.

The only means by determining truth in observable realities is by being versed in them, and versed in the pursuit of questioning what is inconsistent. Some people experience this by debating religion, some by reading classical literature, and most never at all.

What I am trying to say, concisely, is that it's a never ending process of expanding your knowledge and adjusting what you know with what is learned. Like a never-ending trawl of wikipedia, until you actually begin to see how everything makes sense.

Also, you can be assured that it's not just your local community pranking you because you have access to the internet and can talk to users from distant locations (I can vouch that here in the UK, we too generally believe that Asia is west of California).

Now - none of this is foolproof of course, and even having made the journey yourself isn't foolproof - after all, someone may have moved Asia since you last travelled :P In fact, you could be a brain in a jar, and everything else could be virtual.

However, there has to be a point at which you say "I'm going to take this collection of evidence as being good enough". I guess that point varies for different people (well - I'd like to think it does, but I know that many of people believe the first thing that they hear :/)

As this great Youtuber said;

"I don't believe in evolution. I accept evolution because I understand that it is a fact. I don't believe there is a country called New Zealand, I accept that it is a fact. It is not based on faith. I don't have faith in New Zealand. I have a highly reasonable, highly educated guess which is all we can do [as being limited by our senses]."

^ hope that helps. I think it relates to what you're asking.

In a lighter use of the word, faith is trust in our senses. (Solipsism is not trusting any of your senses because they cannot be proven credible.) Solipsism is an irrefutable claim, but that doesn't make it true. Like most irrefutable claims, deciding to ignore them and judge them useless is the best course of action.

Hope this helped.
